strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: exact inversion of diffusion SDEs for editing and continuous-adjoint gradients, and avoiding O(N) storage of the Wiener path is a useful goal.
The use of exponential integrators and the Brownian interval to represent the stochastic term is a reasonable technical direction; Proposition 4.1 provides an explicit exponential-integrator form.
The reversible construction based on a coupling parameter is a plausible extension of reversible ODE solvers to the SDE setting.
The qualitative interpolation examples suggest the proposed method can reconstruct the endpoints exactly in the shown 20-step case.
weaknesses: Technical soundness: As written, Eq. (4.4) does not algebraically invert Eq. (4.3) because the Ψ_h term sign in x_n is inconsistent with the forward equation; if this is a typo, the exact reversibility claim still needs correction. There are also sign/orientation issues in the stochastic-integral derivation (e.g., B.16 vs B.17), so the claimed exact solution is not fully convincingly established.

Terminology: The 'exact solution' in Proposition 4.1 contains an 'Approximated term' and the solver uses a truncated Stratonovich-Taylor expansion; the inversion is only exact for the approximate numerical scheme under a zero-loss model assumption, not for the SDE itself. This distinction should be made clear.

Empirical evidence is far too weak for the central claims: only one qualitative image-interpolation example is shown, with no quantitative inversion metrics (MSE/PSNR/SSIM), no reconstruction error, no comparison to SDE inversion baselines, and no ablation over steps, ζ, or noise.
The memory claim is not measured: the paper asserts no need to store the full Wiener process but provides no memory or runtime comparison against methods such as Wu & De la Torre (2022).
The stability motivation is not supported: no stability analysis, region of convergence, or numerical stability experiments are given, despite stability being a main stated motivation.
Reproducibility is inadequate: no code, no full experimental protocol, no seeds, single dataset/model, and limited hyperparameter details; the results cannot be reliably reproduced or extended.

Significance/originality are limited as presented: the method is a preliminary combination of existing tools (Stratonovich exponential integrator, Brownian interval, reversible coupling), with no downstream editing/adjoint experiment to demonstrate practical advantage.

Ethics/limitations: face datasets and diffusion-based editing raise privacy/bias concerns, but there is no ethics discussion; the limitations section correctly identifies the work as preliminary, but that also confirms the main claims are not yet substantiated.

strengths: The paper attacks a genuinely relevant problem: exact inversion of diffusion SDEs is useful for editing, interpolation, and adjoint-based guided generation, and the observation that SDE inversion is under-explored relative to ODE inversion is reasonable.

The derivation in Proposition 4.1 is technically credible: using variation-of-parameters/exponential integrators on the Stratonovich form of the reverse SDE, then identifying the stochastic integral with a time-changed Brownian motion via Dubins-Schwarz, is a sensible and non-trivial piece of math, and the proof sketch plus Appendix B outline the main steps.

The idea of combining an algebraically reversible (augmented-state, coupling-parameter) integrator with the Brownian interval to avoid materializing the full Wiener path is a reasonable direction and is at least conceptually interesting.
The paper is honest in its Limitations paragraph that this is preliminary, proof-of-concept work, which is appreciated even though it does not substitute for evidence.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is grossly insufficient for a main-track paper. There is exactly one qualitative experiment (image interpolation on a single CelebA-HQ LDM at 20 steps) with no quantitative metric whatsoever: no reconstruction error, PSNR/LPIPS/FID, no comparison of inversion fidelity, no measurement of memory or wall-clock against the alternatives. The central claims (exact inversion, memory efficiency, stability) are therefore unsupported by evidence.

The memory-efficiency claim, which is used to justify the novelty ('first to exactly invert diffusion SDEs without storing the sampled noise from every timestep in memory'), is never measured. No memory footprint or runtime is reported for the proposed method versus path-storing baselines (e.g., Wu & De la Torre, 2022) or versus reversible Heun. The Brownian interval itself stores a tree of noise, so the compute/memory trade-off needs to be demonstrated, not asserted.

The novelty claim is questionable and not adequately defended. The authors themselves note in Related Work that the reversible Heun of Kidger et al. (2021) is applicable to SDEs; a reversible-Heun-based diffusion SDE inverter would also avoid storing the full path. The paper neither compares against this most direct baseline nor explains precisely why the proposed construction is the 'first' such method, so the primary contribution claim is not established.

The word 'exact' conflates algebraic (discrete-map) reversibility with exactness relative to the underlying continuous SDE. Only the discrete update is inverted; the exponential integral is still approximated by a truncated Stratonovich-Taylor expansion, and the discrete trajectory itself is an approximation of the SDE solution. The manuscript does not disentangle these notions, which affects the interpretation of the title and abstract.

Key baseline comparisons are simply missing. DDIM inversion is shown as a straw man, McCallum & Foster (2024) is adapted to DDIM (an ODE), but there is no comparison to the SDE-inversion method of Wu & De la Torre (2022) that is discussed in Related Work, nor to ODE reversible baselines such as EDICT/BDIA/BELM that the paper cites. There is also no multi-seed or multi-image quantitative study, and no ablation over the coupling parameter zeta (only a single value, 0.999, is used).

Motivated applications are never demonstrated. Section 3 motivates the solver by continuous-adjoint guided generation and editing, and the Conclusion lists them as 'potential applications,' but none are tested; the only experiment is interpolation. The claimed advantages (alignment of truncation error in both time directions, stability in both directions) are asserted rather than shown by any stability analysis or numerical experiment.

Internal presentation and technical sloppiness. Equation (2.1) omits the 'dt' term of the drift; Eq. (4.3)'s second line and the rearrangement in (4.4) are hard to follow and appear inconsistent in sign/structure; the proof mixes notation (e.g., Eq. (B.14)/(B.15) give two different final expressions, and x_{T|s} vs x_{0|t} in Appendix A is inconsistent); the symbol zeta is introduced without principled guidance for its selection; the manuscript admits reusing 'W_t' for a different process, which is needlessly confusing.

Reproducibility is weak: a single model, a single dataset, no code release mentioned, no hyperparameter/step-size study, no analysis of how results change with N (only N=20 is ever shown), and no quantitative protocol that others could reproduce or build on.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: exact inversion of diffusion SDEs without storing the full Wiener path in memory, using the Brownian interval to sample Brownian bridges consistently in both directions.
Provides a useful exact-solution representation for diffusion SDEs via exponential integrators and a Dubins-Schwarz time-change (Proposition 4.1), which enables the reversible solver construction.
The qualitative face-interpolation experiment suggests the method can avoid the severe distortion of DDIM inversion at low step counts, supporting the promise of the approach.
The limitations section is honest, explicitly labeling the work as preliminary and identifying future directions such as continuous-adjoint guided generation and stability analysis.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is far too limited for the central claims: only one qualitative figure on face interpolation is provided, with no quantitative metrics such as reconstruction error, FID, PSNR, LPIPS, memory usage, or runtime; no comparison to SDE inversion baselines such as Wu and De la Torre (2022); no ablation over step count, coupling parameter ζ, or datasets.

The technical soundness of the proposed reversible solver is not fully established. There is no consistency or convergence proof showing that the coupled system in Equations (4.3)–(4.4) approximates the underlying diffusion SDE. The auxiliary state x̂ and coupling parameter ζ appear to change the discretization in ways that are not analyzed, and the stability motivation is not backed by stability analysis.
The assumption of a zero-loss data prediction model (x̂_{0|t} = x_{0|t}) is unrealistic and its consequences for exact inversion and sample quality are not discussed.
The claimed memory benefit over storing the entire Wiener process is not measured. Since the main practical advantage is avoiding storage, an empirical memory/runtime comparison is essential.
Reproducibility is limited: no code is released, experimental details are sparse (only a brief appendix), and key solver hyperparameters beyond ζ = 0.999 and 20 steps are not specified.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: equations contain possible typos or sign inconsistencies, notation is sometimes underdefined, related work is placed in an appendix, and proofs are only sketched. The paper reads as a preliminary note rather than a complete conference submission.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: exact/algebraically reversible inversion for diffusion models, with applications to editing and interpolation.

Provides a nontrivial and reasonably rigorous construction: Rex combines exponential integrators, Lawson methods, McCallum-Foster reversible updates, and stochastic Runge-Kutta schemes for ODE and SDE cases, with detailed appendices containing derivations and proofs.

The theoretical results are useful: Theorem 4.1 establishes order inheritance for the ODE case, Theorem 4.2 addresses strong order for the SDE scheme, and the paper carefully discusses stability limitations of prior reversible solvers such as BDIA and O-BELM.

The framework is general and well-connected to prior diffusion solvers: the authors show in Theorem E.1 that the underlying Rex scheme subsumes DDIM, DPM-Solver variants, SDE-DPM-Solver variants, SEEDS-1, and gDDIM, positioning Rex as a reversible counterpart.

The use of splittable PRNG/Brownian interval machinery for SDE reversibility is appropriate and avoids storing the full Brownian trajectory, making the stochastic inversion approach more practical than CycleDiffusion-style storage.

The empirical study, while limited, is informative: it compares against DDIM, EDICT, BDIA, O-BELM on CelebA-HQ and Stable Diffusion v1.5, and reports FID/CLIP/ImageReward plus qualitative interpolation results showing advantages of stochastic Rex variants.
Reproducibility effort is substantial: derivations, noise-schedule inverse functions, implementation details, hyperparameters, hardware, and repositories are provided in appendices.
The paper honestly includes a limitations/failure discussion, e.g. instability of data-prediction ShARK in Appendix J, which is valuable even though it also exposes tensions with the main claims.
weaknesses: The claim of being the first method for exact inversion of diffusion SDEs without storing the entire Brownian trajectory is overstated: reversible Heun for SDEs (Kidger et al., 2021) is already an algebraically reversible SDE solver and can be run with Brownian interval-style noise reconstruction. The paper cites this method but does not reconcile the apparent contradiction, weakening the novelty claim.

The empirical evaluation is limited: only two pretrained models and no error bars/statistical significance. On unconditional CelebA-HQ, Rex is not uniformly better than O-BELM (e.g., O-BELM FID is lower at 10 and 50 steps in Table 1), and ShARK has notably poor FID at 10 steps in Table 4.

The abstract claims Rex works for both data and noise prediction parameterizations, but Appendix J reports a failure case where the data-prediction ShARK formulation overflows and loses algebraic reversibility. This instability is not sufficiently foregrounded in the main paper and undercuts the generality of the claims.

Several notational/theoretical inconsistencies reduce confidence and reproducibility. For example, the backward step in Lemma C.8 writes \hat{X}_n on both sides instead of \hat{X}_{n+1}; Proposition 3.3's backward step passes only W_n even though \Psi also depends on H_n; and the data-prediction proof of Theorem 4.2 writes h as a difference of \sigma^2/\alpha rather than the stated \varrho = \alpha^2/\sigma^2 time variable.

Stability of the stochastic Rex schemes is not formally analyzed in the same way as the ODE case. Given the reported SDE data-prediction instability, this is a notable gap for a method emphasizing exact reversibility in practice.

No direct empirical comparison is provided to general reversible SDE solvers such as reversible Heun, despite those being the closest architectural relatives. The baseline set focuses on diffusion-specific inversion methods, missing a natural comparison point.

The paper does not demonstrate arbitrary high-order convergence for the SDE case, only inherited strong order from a chosen SRK (e.g., ShARK 1.5). Since the abstract emphasizes high order, the SDE limitation should be more clearly stated.
Presentation has multiple typos/corrupted references (e.g., 'diﬀusion quation', 'Kolomogorov', 'Runga-Kutta', malformed citations), which distract from an otherwise technical contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: exact inversion / reversible numerical solvers for diffusion models, including the less-explored reverse-time SDE case.

It provides a clean and potentially useful framework that combines McCallum-Foster reversible solvers with exponential integrators / Lawson methods, and it explicitly shows that Rex subsumes several existing diffusion solvers (e.g., DDIM, DPM-Solver variants, SEEDS-1, gDDIM) as special cases or reversible variants (Appendix E). This unification is a genuine conceptual contribution.

The derivation of the time-changed reverse-time SDE via Dambis-Dubins-Schwarz (Proposition 3.2 / Appendix C.2) appears technically solid and offers a novel reparameterized SDE form for diffusion models.

The construction of a reversible SDE scheme using a shared Brownian realization and space-time Levy area is plausible and avoids explicitly storing the Brownian path, which is a practically relevant goal.
The paper includes detailed appendices with derivations, implementation notes, and some failure-case discussion, indicating substantial technical effort.
Conditional image generation results show that stochastic Rex variants can improve Image Reward over DDIM and other reversible baselines, suggesting potential practical value.
weaknesses: Overclaimed central contribution: the method does not achieve exact distributional inversion of the diffusion SDE; it gives pathwise exact inversion of the numerical discretization for a fixed Brownian realization. Appendix J shows inverted latents have inflated variance and non-Gaussian structure, yet the main paper frames this as exact SDE inversion without adequately qualifying the limitation.

Theoretical gap in Theorem 4.2: the proof does not actually establish that the stochastic Lawson scheme Psi has strong order xi. It assumes Phi has strong order xi and then performs a change of variables, conflating Phi with Psi. No proof is given that the stochastic exponential/Lawson transformation preserves strong order. The theorem as stated is therefore unsupported.

There is no convergence proof for the full reversible Rex SDE scheme. McCallum-Foster convergence is only for ODEs; the paper does not prove that the reversible auxiliary-state SDE scheme converges at all, let alone at the claimed order. This undercuts the claim of rigorous theoretical analysis for the SDE case.

The paper lacks core quantitative evaluations for a reversible solver: no round-trip reconstruction error (MSE/PSNR), no inversion accuracy on real images, and no memory/runtime measurements versus storing the Brownian path. Exact inversion is the central claim, but it is only illustrated qualitatively in Appendix J.

Key baselines are missing. For SDE reversibility, Reversible Heun (Kidger et al., 2021) is a general reversible SDE solver and should be compared, especially since it can also use Brownian interval / splittable PRNGs. For sample quality, DPM-Solver / DPM-Solver++ / SEEDS are not compared, even though Rex (Euler) reduces to DPM-Solver++1 / DDIM. Comparing only to DDIM, EDICT, BDIA, and O-BELM is insufficient to establish state-of-the-art capability.

Empirical results are mixed and do not strongly support the claimed benefits. In unconditional FID (Table 1), Rex (RK4) is worse than O-BELM at all reported step counts, and stochastic Rex is poor at 10/20 steps (e.g., FID 40.79 at 10 steps). Table 4 shows Rex (Midpoint) fails at 10 steps and Rex (ShARK) has FID 59.89 at 10 steps. Conditional results omit FID entirely and show only modest CLIP differences.

The interpolation experiment is only a single qualitative example with no quantitative metric, and ODE variants visibly fail; this is not enough to support claims about better latent-space behavior of stochastic Rex.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work. The reversible mechanism is directly from McCallum-Foster (2024); exponential integrators / Lawson methods for diffusion are related to DPM-Solver and SEEDS; and the Brownian interval / splittable PRNG technique is from prior neural SDE work. The main contribution is an integration of existing tools, which can be valuable but is not as novel as claimed.

Reproducibility is inadequate. There is no Rex code release, no link to an implementation, and the main paper does not specify which prediction parameterization (data vs. noise), step schedule, zeta values, or exact solver configurations were used for each result. Brownian interval / Levy area reconstruction details and seed management are also incomplete.

Presentation quality is uneven. There are multiple notation and equation errors (e.g., Proposition 3.2 defines Y_t with sigma_rho^2 instead of sigma_T^2; inconsistent indices in Proposition 3.3; some malformed references), which make the derivations harder to verify and reduce confidence.

The paper lacks a proper limitations section in the main text. Failure cases, instability of data-prediction variants, and the non-Gaussianity of inverted latents are relegated to appendices and not adequately discussed, despite being central to practical applicability.

Memory claims are not substantiated. The Brownian interval can cache O(N) intervals in practice, so it is unclear whether the method truly avoids O(N) memory; no memory/time comparison is provided. The practical advantage over simply storing Brownian increments is therefore not demonstrated.

strengths: The paper makes a genuinely novel and useful connection between exact inversion of diffusion models and the theory of algebraically reversible ODE/SDE solvers, using Lawson methods to build exponential Runge-Kutta-type schemes (Rex).

It provides a substantial theoretical framework: time-changed/reparameterized ODE and SDE formulations (Propositions 3.1 and 3.2), convergence-order results (Theorem 4.1), a stochastic-order result for the underlying scheme (Theorem 4.2), and a broad comparison showing that Rex subsumes or connects to several known diffusion solvers (Theorem E.1).
The method is designed to support both probability-flow ODEs and reverse-time SDEs, as well as both data- and noise-prediction parameterizations, which increases its practical relevance.
The paper addresses a meaningful problem: exact SDE inversion for diffusion models without storing the entire Brownian path, using a Brownian interval / splittable-PRNG approach from prior work.

The empirical section includes unconditional image generation, conditional text-to-image generation, and interpolation experiments, with competitive conditional Image Reward results for stochastic Rex variants.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed experimental appendices: noise schedules, model names, metrics, hyperparameters, hardware, and the external repositories used.
The limitations and ethics statements are present; the authors acknowledge instability and failure modes in some settings rather than hiding them.
weaknesses: The novelty claim that this is the first exact inversion method for diffusion SDEs without storing the Brownian trajectory is overstated. Reversible Heun for SDEs, together with Brownian interval / splittable PRNG techniques, already provides an algebraically reversible SDE solver of this type; the paper does not compare against this baseline or clearly delineate what is fundamentally new.

The empirical evaluation does not directly quantify the core promised property: exact inversion/reconstruction error. The main tables report FID, CLIP, and Image Reward, but no cycle-consistency or inversion-reconstruction metric is provided, which is important for a paper centered on reversibility.

Unconditional FID results are mixed: Rex (RK4) is worse than O-BELM at 10 and 20 steps, and only Rex (Euler-Maruyama) is best at 50 steps. This weakens the claim that Rex is a broadly superior reversible solver in practice.

The stochastic convergence analysis (Theorem 4.2) is for the underlying reparameterized scheme Psi rather than for the full reversible Rex SDE wrapper. Stability and convergence of the complete reversible SDE solver are not established.

The paper does not report memory or runtime comparisons for the Brownian-interval-based SDE inversion versus path-storage or other reversible SDE methods, so the practical value of avoiding explicit Brownian-path storage is not demonstrated quantitatively.

The presentation is dense and contains several notational inconsistencies and typographical issues (e.g., inconsistent use of symbols in Proposition 3.2 and Lemma C.8, unclear sign/index conventions for the time-changed variables).

No code release is mentioned for the authors' implementation, despite extensive reliance on specific external repositories and numerical details; this limits reproducibility of the exact solver implementation.
The interpolation results are only qualitative, with no quantitative interpolation metric, and the claimed advantage of stochastic Rex over ODE inversion is not systematically established.
